claims.text: What the strip looks like A wide, bizarre QRS with no P wave before it, typically followed by a compensatory pause.
claims.quote: Premature Ventricular Contraction (PVC): Wide, bizarre QRS without preceding P; typically followed by a compensatory pause.

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Timing: premature — earlier than the next expected sinus beat
claims.quote: Premature — i.e. occurs earlier than would be expected for the next sinus impulse

claims.text: QRS: broad (≥ 120 ms) with abnormal morphology
claims.quote: Broad QRS complex (≥ 120 ms) with abnormal morphology

claims.text: P wave: no P wave before the QRS
claims.quote: electrocardiography (ECG) showing a wide QRS complex without a preceding P wave

claims.text: ST and T: discordant (opposite the QRS)
claims.quote: Discordant ST segment and T wave changes.

claims.text: Pause: usually a full compensatory pause
claims.quote: Usually followed by a full compensatory pause

claims.text: With a full compensatory pause, the next normal beat comes after double the preceding R-R interval
claims.quote: With a full compensatory pause, the next normal beat arrives after an interval that is equal to double the preceding R-R interval

claims.text: Retrograde P: the impulse may conduct back through the AV node — an inverted P wave, usually after the QRS
claims.quote: Retrograde capture describes the process whereby the ectopic impulse is conducted retrogradely through the AV node, producing atrial depolarisation. This is visible on the ECG as an inverted P wave (“retrograde P wave“), usually occurring after the QRS complex.

claims.text: Origin: RV PVCs have an LBBB shape (dominant S in V1); LV PVCs have an RBBB shape (dominant R in V1)
claims.quote: PVCs arising from the right ventricle have a left bundle branch block morphology (dominant S wave in V1) PVCs arising from the left ventricle have a right bundle branch block morphology (dominant R wave in V1)

claims.text: Unifocal or multifocal: one focus, identical PVCs; or two or more foci, several QRS shapes
claims.quote: Unifocal — arising from a single ectopic focus; each PVC is identical Multifocal — arising from two or more ectopic foci; multiple QRS morphologies

claims.text: Patterns: bigeminy (every other beat), trigeminy (every third), quadrigeminy (every fourth), couplet (two in a row); three to thirty in a row = NSVT
claims.quote: Bigeminy — every other beat is a PVC Trigeminy — every third beat is a PVC Quadrigeminy — every fourth beat is a PVC Couplet — two consecutive PVCs NSVT — between three and thirty consecutive PVCs

claims.text: “Frequent”: > 5 per minute on a routine ECG, or > 10–30 per hour on ambulatory monitoring
claims.quote: PVCs are said to be “frequent” if there are more than 5 PVCs per minute on the routine ECG, or more than 10-30 per hour during ambulatory monitoring.

claims.text: Causes (mechanism and diagnoses) Mechanism: a ventricular focus fires and bypasses the His-Purkinje system, so the two ventricles activate out of sync — giving a long, abnormal QRS
claims.quote: Ectopic firing of a focus within the ventricles bypasses the His-Purkinje system and depolarises the ventricles directly This disrupts the normal sequence of cardiac activation, leading to asynchronous activation of the two ventricles The consequent interventricular conduction delay produces QRS complexes with prolonged duration and abnormal morphology

claims.text: Frequent or symptomatic PVCs: anxiety, sympathomimetics, beta-agonists, excess caffeine, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, digoxin toxicity, myocardial ischemia
claims.quote: Frequent or symptomatic PVCs may be due to: Anxiety Sympathomimetics Beta-agonists Excess caffeine Hypokalaemia Hypomagnesaemia Digoxin toxicity Myocardial ischemia

claims.text: PVCs increase with stimulants (anxiety, stress, alcohol, caffeine, sympathomimetics), hypoxia and electrolyte abnormalities
claims.quote: VPBs may increase with stimulants (eg, anxiety, stress, alcohol, caffeine, sympathomimetic drugs or medications), hypoxia, or electrolyte abnormalities.

claims.text: Usually benign — but with a prolonged QTc, frequent PVCs can cause “R on T” and trigger torsades
claims.quote: Frequent PVCs are usually benign, except in the context of an prolonged QTc, when they may predispose to malignant ventricular arrhythmias such as Torsades de Pointes by causing “R on T” phenomenon

claims.text: In predisposed patients (e.g., ischemic heart disease, WPW), a PVC can trigger VT, AVNRT or AVRT
claims.quote: In patients with underlying predispositions (e.g. ischaemic heart disease, WPW), a PVC may trigger the onset of a re-entrant tachydysrhythmia — e.g. VT, AVNRT, AVRT

claims.text: Symptoms May be asymptomatic or cause palpitations
claims.quote: VPB may be asymptomatic or cause palpitations.

claims.text: Felt as a missed or skipped beat — what is sensed is the stronger sinus beat after the PVC
claims.quote: VPBs may be experienced as missed or skipped beats; the VPB itself is not sensed but rather the following augmented sinus beat.

claims.text: Very frequent PVCs (especially every second beat) can cause mild hemodynamic symptoms, since the effective rate is halved
claims.quote: When VPBs are very frequent, particularly when they occur at every second heart beat, mild hemodynamic symptoms are possible because the sinus rate has been effectively halved.

claims.text: Treatment No structural heart disease and no or mild symptoms: benign — reassurance only; treat only for bothersome symptoms
claims.quote: In the absence of a structural heart disorder, asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic premature VPBs have a benign prognosis and require no treatment other than reassurance (1). Treatment for VPBs is only required for relief from bothersome symptoms.

claims.text: Bothersome symptoms: beta blockers or nondihydropyridine CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem)
claims.quote: Treatment begins with beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine calcium antagonists (verapamil or diltiazem).

claims.text: After an MI, class I antiarrhythmics raise mortality
claims.quote: Patients in the post-myocardial infarction period have a higher mortality rate when treated with class I antiarrhythmics than with placebo (3).
